Simeon Turnovsky
sim'e-on tur-nov'ske
n. (Simeon Teofil Turnovsky, 1544–1608, senior of the Brethren in Poland and architect of the Sandomierz Consensus)
Hebrew Shimon, hearing; Greek Theophilos, lover of God; Turnovsky, of Turnov, a place-name surname.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Simeon Teofil Turnovsky led the Polish branch of the Unity of the Brethren, which had taken root in Great Poland after the Bohemian expulsions, and he gave much of his life to one object: a working agreement between the Reformed, the Lutherans and the Brethren in Poland. The Consensus of Sandomierz of 1570 was largely his achievement, and he spent the following decades defending it against those on all three sides who thought it conceded too much. He also wrote on church order and kept up correspondence across the Protestant world. The dictionary names him for the character of that work. Turnovsky did not pretend the three churches agreed about the Supper; the Consensus sets out each position and then declares that the parties recognise one another as true churches of Christ. That is harder than either fusion or separation, and it is a model the dictionary commends: say plainly what you believe, say plainly where you differ, and then decide on biblical grounds whether the difference unchurches the other man.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines consensus as agreement of minds, and recognition as the acknowledgment of a thing as valid.

CONSENT', n. Agreement of minds in opinion; accord; concord.

RECOGNI'TION, n. Acknowledgment; formal avowal; knowledge confessed or avowed.

SEN'IOR, n. One older in office or in age; the chief officer of a body of ministers.

COM'MUNION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; mutual participation.

Modern Corruption

The Sandomierz Consensus of 1570 was largely his: three churches naming their differences and recognising each other.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the two easy options. One is fusion, which buys agreement by refusing to state anything; the other is separation, which treats every difference as fatal. Sandomierz did neither: it printed the three positions on the Supper, declined to harmonise them, and then said that these are churches of Christ and will behave toward each other as such.

The principle to recover is that recognition rests on what Christ has received, not on what we find comfortable. “Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God” (Rom 15:7). Walking together presupposes real agreement about real things — “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — and where the attainment is partial, Paul's rule is to hold the ground gained: “let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing” (Phi 3:16).

Usage

"“receive ye one another, as Christ also received us” (Rom 15:7) — Sandomierz, 1570."

"“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — the three positions on the Supper printed, not blended."

"“let us walk by the same rule” (Phi 3:16) — a consensus defended for forty years."
